hmmt-feb-2025-geo-01.title: Isosceles trapezoids
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-01.body:
Extend $DE$ to meet $AC$ at $X$. Since $DE\parallel AB$ and $DF\parallel AC$ (all at $60^\circ$ to $BC$), $ABEX$ and $DFCX$ are isosceles trapezoids with $60^\circ$ base angles. So $AX=BE=14$, $DX=FC=16$, and $\angle AXD=120^\circ$.

By the Law of Cosines in $\triangle ADX$:
$$AD^2=14^2+16^2+14\cdot16=196+256+224=676,\quad AD=26.$$

**Answer: 26**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-01.title: Coordinates
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-01.body:
Put $B=(0,0)$, $C=(45,0)$, so $A=\left(\frac{45}2,\frac{45\sqrt3}2\right)$. $E=(14,0)$, $F=(29,0)$, so $D=\left(\frac{43}2,\frac{15\sqrt3}2\right)$. Then
the horizontal difference between $A$ and $D$ is $\frac{45-43}2=1$ and the vertical difference is $\frac{45\sqrt3-15\sqrt3}2=15\sqrt3$, so $AD^2=1+675=676$ and $AD=26$.

**Answer: 26**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-02.title: Diagonals share a midpoint
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-02.body:
Let the cave height be $H$; the stalactite tips are at heights $H-16$ and $H-36$, the stalagmite tips at $25$ and $49$.

If the two stalactite tips were adjacent vertices of the square, the side between them would have vertical extent $20$, and the opposite side (the stalagmite tips) would have the same vertical extent; but $49-25=24\neq 20$. So the stalactite tips are opposite vertices, and so are the stalagmite tips.

The diagonals of a square bisect each other, so the midpoints' heights agree: $H-26=37$, so $H=63$.

**Answer: 63**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-02.title: Check the square exists
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-02.body:
With $H=63$ the tip heights are $47, 27$ (stalactites) and $25, 49$ (stalagmites), all centred at height $37$. The stalactite diagonal has vertical extent $20$, the stalagmite diagonal $24$. For perpendicular diagonals of equal length $L$, a vector $(u,20)$ and its rotation $(-20,u)$ (up to sign) needs $|u|=24$: diagonal $(24,20)$ and $(20,-24)$ have equal lengths and are perpendicular. So we can place the structures horizontally to form a square, confirming $H=63$.

**Answer: 63**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-03.title: Distances to the sides
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-03.body:
The square has area $1+2+3+4=10$, side $s=\sqrt{10}$. The distances from $P$ to the sides are $\frac{2\cdot\text{area}}{s}$, i.e. $\{x,2x,3x,4x\}$ with $x=\frac{2}{\sqrt{10}}$. Opposite distances sum to $s$, so the opposite pairs are $\{x,4x\}$ and $\{2x,3x\}$ (both sum to $5x=\sqrt{10}$).

Each vertex distance is the hypotenuse with legs one distance from each pair, going around: legs $(x,2x),(2x,4x),(4x,3x),(3x,x)$:
$$PA\cdot PB\cdot PC\cdot PD=\sqrt5x\cdot\sqrt{20}x\cdot5x\cdot\sqrt{10}x=50\sqrt{10}\,x^4=50\sqrt{10}\cdot\frac{4}{25}=8\sqrt{10}.$$

**Answer: $8\sqrt{10}$**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-03.title: Coordinates
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-03.body:
Take the square $[0,\sqrt{10}]^2$ and $P=(a,b)$ with $\{a,\sqrt{10}-a\}=\left\{\frac2{\sqrt{10}},\frac8{\sqrt{10}}\right\}$ and $\{b,\sqrt{10}-b\}=\left\{\frac4{\sqrt{10}},\frac6{\sqrt{10}}\right\}$; say $a=\frac2{\sqrt{10}}$, $b=\frac4{\sqrt{10}}$. The squared distances to the corners are $\frac{4+16}{10}=2$, $\frac{64+16}{10}=8$, $\frac{64+36}{10}=10$, $\frac{4+36}{10}=4$. Product of distances $=\sqrt{2\cdot8\cdot10\cdot4}=\sqrt{640}=8\sqrt{10}$. Any other assignment is a reflection of this one.

**Answer: $8\sqrt{10}$**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-04.title: Similar configurations
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-04.body:
Let $P,Q$ be the centres of $S_3,S_2$. Given $S_3$, the position of an inscribed $S_2$ is determined by the angle between their diameters; likewise for $S_2$ and $S_1$. Since the diameters of $S_1$ and $S_3$ are parallel, the angle between $S_1,S_2$ equals the angle between $S_2,S_3$, so $S_3\cup S_2$ is similar to $S_2\cup S_1$. Hence $r_2^2=r_1r_3=10$, $r_2=\sqrt{10}$.

Let $V$ be an endpoint of $S_2$'s diameter (on $S_3$'s arc). Then $PV=10$, $QV=\sqrt{10}$, and $PQ\perp QV$, so $PQ^2=100-10=90$. Also $QC\perp AB$ with $QC=\sqrt{10}$, so $PC^2=90-10=80$. Therefore
$$AC\cdot CB=(10+PC)(10-PC)=100-80=20.$$

**Answer: 20**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-04.title: Power of a point
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-04.body:
$AC\cdot CB$ is the power of $C$ with respect to the full circle of $S_3$: $100-PC^2$. Since $QC\perp AB$ and $PQ\perp$ (diameter of $S_2$), $PC^2=PQ^2-r_2^2=(100-r_2^2)-r_2^2=100-2r_2^2$. So $AC\cdot CB=2r_2^2=2\cdot10=20$, using $r_2=\sqrt{r_1r_3}=\sqrt{10}$ from the similarity.

**Answer: 20**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-05.title: Use the antipode of $A$
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-05.body:
Let $A'$ be the antipode of $A$ on the circumcircle. Then $\angle AXA'=90^\circ$ and $\angle AXP=90^\circ$, so $X,P,A'$ are collinear.

$\angle BA'C=180^\circ-60^\circ=120^\circ=\angle BPC$, and $A'B=A'C$, so $P$ lies on the circle centred at $A'$ through $B,C$ (the arc of points seeing $BC$ at $120^\circ$ inside the triangle). Its radius is $A'B=\frac{6}{\sqrt3}=2\sqrt3$ (the circumradius), so $A'P=2\sqrt3$ and $AA'=4\sqrt3$.

In right triangle $AXA'$: $XA'=\sqrt{48-25}=\sqrt{23}$. So $XP=XA'-PA'=\sqrt{23}-2\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{23}-2\sqrt3$**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-06.title: The circumcenter quadrilateral is similar
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-06.body:
Let $O_A,O_B,O_C,O_D$ be the circumcenters of the triangles missing $A,B,C,D$. Each side of $O_AO_BO_CO_D$ lies on a perpendicular bisector of a side or diagonal of $ABCD$ (e.g. $O_BO_C$ is the perpendicular bisector of $AD$), so its sides are perpendicular to the corresponding sides of $ABCD$; hence $O_AO_BO_CO_D$ is a trapezoid similar to $ABCD$.

**Height of $ABCD$.** Draw through $B$ a parallel to $AD$ meeting $CD$ at $X$: $BX=4$, $BC=8$, $XC=8$. Triangle $BXC$ is isosceles with base $BX=4$, so its height from $C$ is $\sqrt{64-4}=2\sqrt{15}$ and its area is $4\sqrt{15}$; the height from $B$ onto $XC$ is $h=\frac{2\cdot 4\sqrt{15}}8=\sqrt{15}$.

**Height of the new trapezoid.** Its parallel sides lie on the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $CD$, so its height is the horizontal distance between the midpoints of $AB$ and $CD$: $\frac{19}2-\left(\sqrt{16-15}+\frac{11}2\right)=3$.

Ratio $\frac{3}{\sqrt{15}}$; area of $ABCD=\frac{11+19}2\sqrt{15}=15\sqrt{15}$. So the answer is $\frac{9}{15}\cdot15\sqrt{15}=9\sqrt{15}$.

**Answer: $9\sqrt{15}$**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-06.title: Coordinates
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-06.body:
Put $D=(0,0)$, $C=(19,0)$, $A=(1,\sqrt{15})$, $B=(12,\sqrt{15})$ (check: $DA=4$, $BC=\sqrt{49+15}=8$). Computing the four circumcenters and the area of their convex hull numerically gives $34.8569\ldots=9\sqrt{15}$.

**Answer: $9\sqrt{15}$**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-07.title: Homothetic bisector triangles
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-07.body:
Let the internal and external bisectors of $\angle BAC$ meet line $BC$ at $D,E$, and those of $\angle BPC$ meet it at $D',E'$. The angle condition $\angle ABP=\angle ACP$ implies that $AD\parallel PD'$ and $AE\parallel PE'$, so triangles $ADE$ and $PD'E'$ are homothetic (from a point on $BC$), and the ratio of heights to $BC$ is $\frac{D'E'}{DE}$.

By the angle bisector theorem: $BD=7\cdot\frac6{14}=3$, $BE=7\cdot\frac6{2}=21$, so $DE=24$; $BD'=7\cdot\frac13=\frac73$, $BE'=7\cdot\frac11=7$, so $D'E'=\frac{28}3$.

$\frac{[BPC]}{[ABC]}=\frac{28/3}{24}=\frac7{18}$.

**Answer: $\frac7{18}$**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-07.title: Cyclic quadrilateral, Ceva and Menelaus
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-07.body:
Let $D=AP\cap BC$, $E=BP\cap AC$, $F=CP\cap AB$. $\angle FBE=\angle ECF$ means $BCEF$ is cyclic, so $AE\cdot AC=AF\cdot AB$, $\frac{AE}{AF}=\frac34$; let $AE=3x$, $AF=4x$. Triangles $PFB\sim PEC$ give $\frac{BF}{CE}=\frac{BP}{CP}=\frac12$: $\frac{6-4x}{8-3x}=\frac12\Rightarrow x=\frac45$. So $AF=\frac{16}5$, $FB=\frac{14}5$, $AE=\frac{12}5$, $EC=\frac{28}5$.

Ceva: $\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AE}{EC}\cdot\frac{BF}{FA}=\frac{12}{28}\cdot\frac{14}{16}=\frac38$, so $BD=\frac{21}{11}$. Menelaus on $\triangle ADC$ with line $B,P,E$: $\frac{AP}{PD}=\frac{CB}{BD}\cdot\frac{AE}{EC}=\frac{11}{3}\cdot\frac{3}{7}=\frac{11}7$. Hence $\frac{PD}{AD}=\frac7{18}=\frac{[BPC]}{[ABC]}$.

**Answer: $\frac7{18}$**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-08.title: Reflect $D$ over $M$
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-08.body:
Let $D'$ be the reflection of $D$ across $M$. Then $ADED'$ is a parallelogram, so $D'A\parallel ED$ (i.e. parallel to $AB$) and $D'A=ED=2$. So $D'$ lies on line $AB$ with $D'A=2$ on the side away from $B$, giving $D'B=6$.

Power of the point $D'$ with respect to the circle: line $D'MD$ meets it at $M,D$, and line $D'AB$ at $A,B$. With $MD=D'M=x$: $x\cdot2x=2\cdot6$, so $x=\sqrt6$. (The radius is not needed.)

**Answer: $\sqrt6$**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-09.title: Antipodes on line $CD$
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-09.body:
Let $P$ be the antipode of $A$ in circle $(AXD)$ and $Q$ the antipode of $B$ in $(BXC)$. Since $\angle PDA=90^\circ$, $P$ lies on line $CD$; likewise $Q$. Since $\angle PXA=90^\circ=\angle BXA$, $P$ lies on line $BX$; similarly $Q$ lies on $AX$.

$AP=26$, so $DP=\sqrt{26^2-24^2}=10$; $BQ=30$, so $CQ=\sqrt{30^2-24^2}=18$. With $AB=x$, $PQ=x-28$. Quadrilateral $ABQP$ has perpendicular diagonals $AQ\perp BP$ (they lie along $AX\perp BX$), so $AB^2+PQ^2=AP^2+BQ^2$:
$$x^2+(x-28)^2=676+900\implies x^2-28x-396=0\implies x=14\pm4\sqrt{37}.$$
The acuteness condition rules out $14-4\sqrt{37}$, leaving $AB=14+4\sqrt{37}$.

**Answer: $14+4\sqrt{37}$**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-09.title: Circumcentres and similar triangles
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-09.body:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $O_1,O_2$ the circumcentres of $AXD$, $BXC$. $O_1M$ and $O_2M$ are the perpendicular bisectors of $AX$ and $BX$, so $\angle O_1MO_2=90^\circ$. $O_1,O_2$ are at height $12$ (on the perpendicular bisectors of $AD$, $BC$); their feet $P_1,P_2$ on $AB$ satisfy $P_1A=\sqrt{13^2-12^2}=5$, $P_2B=\sqrt{15^2-12^2}=9$. With $AB=2x$: $MP_1=x-5$, $MP_2=x-9$, and $\triangle MP_1O_1\sim\triangle O_2P_2M$ gives $(x-5)(x-9)=144$, so $x=7+2\sqrt{37}$ and $AB=14+4\sqrt{37}$.

**Answer: $14+4\sqrt{37}$**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-10.title: Midpoints of the long diagonals
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-10.body:
Label the hexagon $ABCDEF$ with $AB=45$, $BC=66$, $CD=63$, $DE=55$, $EF=54$, $FA=77$. Opposite sides lie on opposite (parallel) faces, so $AB\parallel DE$, $BC\parallel EF$, $CD\parallel FA$. Let $O$ be the prism's centre and $M,N,P$ the midpoints of $AD,BE,CF$.

$MN$ is the midline between $AB$ and $DE$, so $MN=\frac{|55-45|}2=5$, and plane $OMN$ is the mid-plane between the two faces containing $AB,DE$. Similarly $NP=\frac{66-54}2=6$, $PM=\frac{77-63}2=7$, and $OM,ON,OP$ are pairwise perpendicular (each pair spans a mid-plane, and the three mid-planes are mutually perpendicular).

With $x=OM$, $y=ON$, $z=OP$: $x^2+y^2=25$, $y^2+z^2=36$, $z^2+x^2=49$, so $x^2=19$, $y^2=6$, $z^2=30$. Heron: $[MNP]=\sqrt{9\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2}=6\sqrt6$. The tetrahedron $OMNP$ has volume $\frac16xyz=\frac13[MNP]\,d$, so
$$d=\frac{\sqrt{19\cdot6\cdot30}}{2\cdot6\sqrt6}=\frac{\sqrt{19\cdot 30}}{12}=\sqrt{\frac{570}{144}}=\sqrt{\frac{95}{24}}.$$

**Answer: $\sqrt{\frac{95}{24}}$**

hmmt-feb-2025-geo-10.title: Translate the plane
hmmt-feb-2025-geo-10.body:
A plane through the centre cuts a centrally symmetric hexagon with sides $a,b,c,a,b,c$. Translating it changes the sides to $(a-t_a,\,b+t_b,\,c-t_c,\,a+t_a,\,b-t_b,\,c+t_c)=(45,66,63,55,54,77)$, so $t_a=5$, $t_b=6$, $t_c=7$. If the translation moves the plane's intercepts on the three axes by $d_x,d_y,d_z$, then by Pythagoras $t_a^2=d_y^2+d_z^2$, $t_b^2=d_z^2+d_x^2$, $t_c^2=d_x^2+d_y^2$, so $(d_x^2,d_y^2,d_z^2)=(6,30,19)$. The distance from the centre to the plane is the height of the right-corner tetrahedron with legs $d_x,d_y,d_z$:
$$\frac1{d^2}=\frac16+\frac1{30}+\frac1{19}=\frac{24}{95},\qquad d=\sqrt{\frac{95}{24}}.$$

**Answer: $\sqrt{\frac{95}{24}}$**
